description:
Somos Sora, un equipo interdisciplinario de cinco estudiantes de Ciencia de Datos, Programación, Psicología Social, Sociología, Medicina y Química.

Nos unimos para participar en el desafío de la NASA sobre monitoreo de la salud de astronautas en misiones espaciales. Buscamos integrar tecnología, conocimiento científico y una perspectiva humana para desarrollar una solución innovadora que contribuya a la salud y el bienestar de quienes exploran el espacio.
summary:
We developed MATE, an astronaut health monitoring prototype designed around AI as the primary interface. Each crew member has Orbit, a personal assistant designed to put health records in context, flag changes before anyone asks, and show the evidence behind each alert.

The demo follows a simulated day in space, with alerts triggered by mission events. When a new sleep record arrives, Orbit notices that Lucía slept less than her personal baseline for the third night in a row. She can open the record directly from the alert, and the medical team on Earth can review the same trend. The demo also shows lab result notifications and exercise reminders.

The proposed architecture would combine data from wearable sensors, environmental sensors, and spacecraft cameras. Specialized AI agents would help interpret the data based on its source and mission context. This would extend monitoring to nutrition, personal radiation exposure, and cabin conditions.

Monitoring alone is not enough if changes go unnoticed. MATE aims to reduce the time crews spend checking scattered records and help them see what changed, when it happened, and where the information came from. Orbit draws attention to what matters. The crew and medical team make the decisions.
details:
When we started working on MATE, we asked ourselves a simple question. Why should an astronaut have to check several screens just to find out something changed? That’s where Orbit came from. Orbit is a companion that can give astronauts a heads-up without waiting for them to open a chat, then take them straight to the record that shows what happened.

In the demo, Lucía starts her day and Orbit tells her she’s slept less than usual for the third night in a row. She can open her sleep history right from the alert, and the medical team on Earth can see the same chart. The operations team, on the other hand, sees the schedule and equipment bookings but doesn’t have access to health records. We also show how Orbit reminds Lucía about a workout and lets her know when a lab result is ready.

For now, those alerts run on simulated data and rules. In a future version, MATE would bring together data from sensors worn by the astronauts and from sensors and cameras on the spacecraft. Specialized AI agents would help interpret that data, and Orbit could explain what changed and where the information came from. We want the crew to spend less time looking for information and more time acting on what matters, while keeping medical decisions in human hands.

We built the app with React, TypeScript, and Vite and tested it with Vitest and in Chrome. We didn’t connect any real hardware. What we most wanted to explore was what it would feel like to have this assistant on board. That’s why we gave each astronaut a different companion and used a mission clock so alerts show up when the information actually arrives, not before.
